boundary_note: Bounded first pass for the frozen Franklin record (November 30, 1864) in the Franklin-Nashville Campaign [September-December 1864]. Spring Hill (TN035) precedes it; the Nashville record (TN038) begins December 15. Campaign-wide marches, returns, reinforcements and multi-action loss totals are context; they are not assigned to one record or added across records. Draft claims do not alter model inputs.

claims.rationale: No inspected return establishes matched personnel at a common opening boundary. The frozen side-specific numerical strength bounds are blank (missing_numeric_strength). No figure in this pass is adopted as a simultaneous opening force.

claims.value: The frozen force text reads the IV and XXIII Corps against the Army of Tennessee with no numbers; the live field reads zeros. Cox says Hood attacked with Cheatham's and Stewart's corps, Johnson's division of Lee's corps being the only one of that corps yet up, and that the two Twenty-third Corps divisions could not reach the river on the right, so Kimball's division was added. Hood says Stewart's and Cheatham's corps attacked with Johnson's division engaged later.
claims.rationale: Formations only; the campaign returns in Cox's pp.11–19 are dated November 6 and October 31 and are not a Franklin count. None is adopted as a matched opening strength; live zeros are not measured absence.

claims.value: NPS says Schofield formed his line in works thrown up in the spring of 1863. Cox says the Twenty-third Corps began building breastworks that morning and had a strong intrenchment by noon, with an osage-orange hedge thinned into a palisade before Stiles. Hood says the works were so hastily constructed that there was only slight abatis on part of the line and none on the extreme right.
claims.rationale: The accounts differ on whether the line used 1863 works or works built that day; phase left unresolved.

claims.value: Cox says Schofield found on arrival that no pontoons had come, that improvised planking gave two passable bridges by noon, and that the trains were nearly all across by 3 p.m. NPS says Schofield wished to stay at Franklin to repair the bridges and get his trains over. Hood says he did not use his artillery during the day because women and children remained in the town; Cox, writing from his own observation, says Hood's recollection is in error.
claims.rationale: Transport statements from an interested participant history; the artillery-use conflict is preserved as a dispute.

claims.value: Cox says Schofield put Cox in command of both Twenty-third Corps divisions to intrench the line and himself watched from the fort north of the river; that Wagner, contrary to his orders, sent a command to his two advanced brigades to fight; and that White and Opdycke charged without waiting for orders. Hood says the line advanced at 4 p.m. The frozen commanders are Major General Schofield and General Hood.
claims.rationale: Direction and fault are attributed as the sources state; Cox was the officer commanding the line, an interested participant, and his account of Wagner rests on two unnamed officers. No listed commander receives automatic sole credit.

claims.value: The frozen and live results read Union victory. Hood says his troops carried the first line and parts of the interior line and that the enemy abandoned his works near midnight, leaving his dead and wounded; in December he wrote that they failed to carry the interior line. Cox says Schofield ordered the withdrawal at eleven after the front was quiet.
claims.rationale: Retain the original result and engagement interval; later movements and campaign contribution are different measures. No new probabilities or individual causal credit.

claims.value: The frozen casualty text reads 8,587 (US 2,326; CS 6,261); the live field reads 9,933 (US 2,633; CS 7,300). Hood gives his loss in killed, wounded and prisoners as 4,500, about 1,000 prisoners taken, and Union dead indicating a loss 'equal or near our own'. Cox says Hood's computation gave 7,547 since the opening of the campaign and 6,300 in this battle, including 700 prisoners; Union losses were 2,326, more than 1,000 in Wagner's two brigades. NPS counts six Confederate generals killed or mortally wounded; Cox counts twelve generals disabled. Cox gives 22 flags taken by Reilly's division and 10 by Opdycke's brigade; Hood, per Cox, says thirteen.
claims.rationale: Original casualty returns were not inspected; preserve totals, categories, cutoffs and differences. No canonical reconciliation or casualty-based opening count; related actions must not be added without resolving population overlap. Hood's campaign figure (7,547) includes Columbia and Spring Hill and is not a Franklin count.

open_questions: Schofield's No. 96, Cox's No. 97 report and journal, Stanley's, Wagner's, Opdycke's, Reilly's and the other Union reports, Stewart's and the Confederate division reports, the Nos. 2 and 7 returns, Cox's Appendix D (Franklin correspondence) and the Confederate casualty returns Cox cites remain deferred.

NPS/CWSAC (the live NPS page and the frozen Arnold rows) is one family. Jacob D. Cox's The March to the Sea; Franklin and Nashville (1882) is an interested history by the commander of the Twenty-third Corps' Third Division (and, at Franklin, of both divisions of that corps) that draws on official papers. Corse's, French's, R. S. Granger's, Doolittle's, Sinclair's, Forrest's, Hood's and Rousseau's reports, printed in Official Records Series I, Volumes XXXIX part 1 and XLV part 1, are separate families of interested accounts; each volume is a shared container, not an additional witness. Report dates are not event times or proof of contemporary knowledge.
No automatic commander attribution, causal campaign score, morale/readiness number or battle/campaign double counting.
